title: MLK assassination records · the 2025 release
summary: The National Archives hosts records related to the assassination of Martin Luther King Jr. released following Executive Order 14176. Its release page dates the July 21, 2025 release and links the individual files. This is the official starting point for the release, not a private collection of supposed secret conclusions.
why: Public access gives readers a way to inspect the documentary record rather than rely entirely on a headline or a viral excerpt. Read this collection beside King’s own writing and historical scholarship so that institutional surveillance does not become the only frame through which his life is understood.
caution: The release is not a promise that every related record is public or that every allegation inside a file is true. NARA notes that some information may be withheld under law. A new release date does not make the events inside recent.
question: What can this particular document establish, and what would require another source?

title: COINTELPRO · FBI Vault records
summary: The FBI Vault provides publicly released records connected with COINTELPRO. The collection is a route into documents about a federal counterintelligence program; use its file groupings and pages to identify the particular operation you are examining.
why: The documents help readers examine the relationship between political activity, surveillance and institutional power. Reading an agency’s own language can reveal its priorities, but those priorities must be studied critically rather than accepted as neutral descriptions of the people targeted.
caution: Government terminology can be stigmatizing and allegations can be uncorroborated. Record the file number and page when taking notes, and distinguish an agency proposal, an action reported, and an outcome independently established.
question: Whose definition of a threat is shaping the document?

title: King’s own words · the Papers Project
summary: The Martin Luther King Jr. Papers Project explains the scholarly effort to collect and publish King’s correspondence, speeches, sermons and other writings. Its editorial work provides a starting point for reading the thinker and organizer in his own words.
why: Place King’s intellectual work alongside records produced about him. That comparison helps prevent a life devoted to religion, justice, organizing and peace from being reduced to a surveillance file or one famous speech.
caution: A project overview is a research gateway, not the full text of every volume. Follow individual document citations and editorial notes; an excerpt may leave out the audience and occasion that shaped the original.
question: How does King’s own explanation change the question you brought to an agency record?

title: Freedmen’s Bureau · rebuilding lives after slavery
summary: NARA’s Freedmen’s Bureau research guide leads to records of the Bureau of Refugees, Freedmen, and Abandoned Lands. The materials support research into life after emancipation, including family connections, labor, education and the work of federal offices.
why: These records can bring family history and institutional history into conversation. A name, contract or school record can illuminate the everyday work of pursuing freedom, while also revealing the constraints that followed slavery’s legal end.
caution: Coverage varies by place and office. A missing entry is not proof that a person or event did not exist. Administrative records often preserve an official’s viewpoint and may use harmful historical language.
question: What choices and constraints become visible in this everyday record?

title: Born in Slavery · the Federal Writers’ Project narratives
summary: The Library of Congress collection brings together narratives gathered from formerly enslaved people through the Federal Writers’ Project in 1936–1938, alongside photographs and contextual essays. It is a significant source collection for examining memories of slavery.
why: Personal recollections offer perspectives that official accounts can fail to preserve. The collection also makes the process of recording history visible: whose questions were asked, whose words were transcribed, and how a published account came into being.
caution: These interviews were recorded decades after emancipation and shaped by interviewer relationships and transcription choices. Read the collection’s essays before treating a transcript as an unmediated recording.
question: How might the interview setting have influenced what could be said?

title: Civil Rights History Project · video testimony
publisher: Library of Congress and Smithsonian NMAAHC
summary: This joint project preserves recorded interviews with participants in the civil rights movement. The collection pairs video testimony with contextual material and provides a way to hear people describe organizing, risk, relationships and change.
why: Voice, pauses and emphasis can add dimensions that a written outline misses. The interviews invite readers to connect major milestones with the local work and personal relationships that helped make collective action possible.
caution: An interview is a situated recollection, not a complete account of every event. Identify the speaker, interview date and questions, and compare an account with other sources before generalizing.
question: What does this person’s account add to the familiar public timeline?

title: The House gag rule · silencing antislavery petitions
publisher: U.S. House of Representatives, History, Art & Archives
summary: The House historian’s account explains the 1836 rule that prevented consideration of antislavery petitions and the struggle over its repeal. It links readers to the institutional history of a real restriction on what could be debated.
why: This entry belongs in the room because it concerns a documented restriction on public argument. It helps distinguish actual historical suppression from a broad suggestion that every overlooked document was once legally banned.
caution: This is an institutional historical explanation with links to an object and related resources. Follow those references when you need the precise wording of a resolution or a specific vote.
question: Who gained power when a petition could be submitted but not considered?

title: Brown v. Board of Education · the 1954 opinion
summary: The National Archives presents the Supreme Court’s 1954 school-desegregation decision with a transcript and links to the original record. The opinion addresses equal protection and the constitutional status of racial segregation in public education.
why: Reading the decision itself gives substance to a familiar milestone. Compare its reasoning with the practical work required to change schools; a legal ruling and the lived experience of implementation are related but different parts of the story.
caution: The decision is not a complete history of every community’s school struggle. Distinguish Brown I from the later implementation decision and from subsequent events.
question: What does the court require, and what remains to be accomplished outside the written opinion?

title: Tulsa 1921 · the Oklahoma commission report
summary: The Oklahoma Historical Society hosts the report of the Oklahoma Commission to Study the Tulsa Race Riot of 1921. The report examines the destruction of Greenwood and brings historical research, testimony and findings into a public document.
why: The report invites a careful study of a community’s achievement, the violence directed against it, and the long work of recovering a public record. Follow evidence and source notes rather than reducing Greenwood to one dramatic statistic or image.
caution: The report contains accounts of violence and historical terminology. Distinguish the date of the events from the later commission’s investigation, and examine how individual findings were supported.
question: How does recovering a record change a community’s ability to ask for recognition or repair?

title: Challenged books · inspect the documented lists
summary: ALA’s dated most-challenged lists document attempts to restrict access to books and include works by Black authors. Use the relevant year and its description when researching a particular title, rather than treating a listing as proof of a nationwide ban.
why: Cultural argument often begins with whose stories may be available. A documented challenge is a useful starting point for examining a specific dispute, while preserving the distinction between an attempt to restrict access and a completed removal.
caution: A challenge and a ban are different. Outcomes and definitions vary by institution and report. This gateway does not establish that every title in the DSB Library has been banned.
question: What exactly was challenged, where, when, and with what documented result?

title: Omar Ibn Said · an enslaved scholar’s Arabic manuscript
summary: The Omar Ibn Said Collection includes an 1831 autobiographical manuscript written in Arabic by a West African scholar while enslaved in the United States, alongside related documents in Arabic and English. It connects literacy, language and the African diaspora.
why: The manuscript challenges the assumption that people brought into slavery arrived without intellectual or religious traditions. Reading its context alongside translations makes room for a life that does not fit a single familiar narrative of American literacy.
caution: A translation is an interpretation and may differ across scholars. Read the collection’s context and distinguish the original manuscript from later descriptions, translations and claims about belief.
question: What changes when we begin the story with knowledge the writer already possessed?

title: Conversation on the Omar Ibn Said Collection
summary: The Library of Congress provides a recorded conversation about the Omar Ibn Said Collection. It offers a video route into the manuscript’s context and the work of interpreting a multilingual historical collection.
why: A curator or scholarly discussion can help readers approach a document with better questions. Use this conversation as a companion to the original collection, not a substitute for examining the manuscript and its editorial context.
caution: Distinguish statements made by speakers from the original document’s words. If you quote a discussion, record the speaker and timestamp, then follow any source references that support the claim.
question: Which question from the conversation would you bring back to the manuscript?
